operand.headline: Breaking: MNPD Accessed Hundreds of Thousands of Flock ALPR Cameras, Seemingly in Blatant Violation of Nashville Law
operand.dek: Other agencies conducted over a thousand searches for MNPD through hundreds of thousands of ALPRs installed without the public's consent

body.caption: Rep. Thomas Massie's parody "Don't Flock on Me" flag, posted to X alongside his call to withhold federal funds from municipalities running Flock Safety cameras.

tokens.c: over 1,000 vehicle searches using technology like Flock Safety's automated license plate reader (ALPR) cameras

tokens: , despite being barred by Metro Council from using surveillance technology it has not been explicitly authorized to use except under explicit, limited circumstances.

tokens.c: The searches conducted on behalf of MNPD leveraged systems that draw data from enormous networks of ALPRs operated by private companies like Flock Safety, which use at least hundreds of thousands of devices across the United States to collect location data from American drivers without consent.
It is not possible with the data available to tell if any of these searches used warrants

tokens: That MNPD reaches into these systems is not itself new.

tokens.c: What the data reveals is the staggering scale at which it happens, and that it happens almost entirely outside the reach of any safeguard, audit, or public records law. MNPD has kept drawing on that access without the council authorization required by Metro law, and without ever disclosing to the public how often it was doing so.
This is unfolding inside a national crisis that Flock, one of many purveyors of AI-powered corporate mass surveillance, is racing to contain, not a contained local dispute.
Nearly 100 municipalities have walked away from Flock contracts since 2021

q.web-msscu50s0: walked away from the company since 2021 at roughly 98

tokens.c: many citing, in the LAPD's words, serious concerns about civil liberties and civil rights, particularly regarding privacy and the data being collected

q.web-msscu50t1: serious concerns around civil liberties and civil rights issues, particularly around privacy

tokens.c: The same failure this piece documents in Nashville has already surfaced elsewhere, from the other direction.
Mountain View discovered that Flock had allowed outside agencies to access its cameras without the city's knowledge, with its police chief calling that access "frankly unacceptable."
Dayton, Ohio found its own cameras had been searched more than 7,100 times for immigration enforcement, explicitly banned under the city's own policy.

q.web-msscu50t2: searched more than 7,100 times for immigration enforcement purposes

tokens.c: Nashville's numbers are not an isolated finding. They are one more data point inside a crisis that is still accelerating.

It was previously thought that MNPD's pattern of deploying surveillance technology without council authorization went back to September 2022, when it quietly entered into an unauthorized contract with the camera-network company Fusus, and continued through May 2026, when it launched a Drone as First Responder program without the public hearing or council vote Metro law requires beforehand.

The Flock searches reviewed for this story push that timeline back even further, to early 2022, when other departments' logs already show ALPR searches run on MNPD's behalf, likely in violation of Nashville's 2017 surveillance ordinance, which explicitly named ALPRs among the technologies requiring council approval.
tokens.note: Author's own observation from reviewing the Have I Been Flocked dataset; not an independently sourced count.

tokens.c: Nashville People's Journal (NPJ) will extract data as part of a prolonged analysis of MNPD's protracted history of AI-powered corporate mass surveillance outside the bounds of all "safeguards" imposed on them. NPJ strongly supports other local media looking into these extremely concerning revelations.

body.text: MNPD Does Not Have Blanket Authorization to Access Surveillance Data

tokens.c: Metro code permits surveillance technology without Council approval only in narrow circumstances.

tokens: The exception applies when the technology is

tokens.c: used on a temporary basis for a criminal investigation supported by reasonable suspicion, pursuant to a lawfully issued search warrant, or under exigent circumstances as defined in case law

q.web-mss9pyxy9: used on a temporary basis for the purpose of a criminal investigation supported by reasonable suspicion, or pursuant to a lawfully issued search warrant, or under exigent circumstances as defined in case law

tokens.c: MNPD has no direct access to Flock's LPR network.

q.web-mss9pyxy5: does not have direct access to Flock’s LPR network

tokens.c: Any formal access to it, even "borrowing access" from another department, outside those aforementioned limited uses, is likely in blatant violation of the so-called "surveillance ordinance."

tokens.c: Even that critique sits inside the guardrails framework the previous section describes: the ACLU is arguing Flock's reforms are not strong enough guardrails, not that guardrails are the wrong tool. Increasingly, it appears that the only way to protect surveillance data from getting into the wrong hands is not to have data at all.
The information available on HaveIBeenFlocked.com raises more questions than it answers.
Did MNPD, or the agencies searching on its behalf, have warrants authorizing use of these databases, or were they sidestepping local council restrictions entirely?

These searches span both a state agency and multiple municipal departments. Which type of requesting agency accounts for the larger share of the total, and whether that share is concentrated in a handful of standing relationships or spread across many independent requests, is not yet established.
Were any of these searches conducted for personal reasons, as has been documented nationally in the cases above? That remains unconfirmed for any specific search in this dataset.
The pattern documented here shows MNPD reaching Flock's network through other agencies' systems, without the council approval Metro law requires and without disclosing the practice to the public.
